edges.description: Fibronectin that never reaches the extracellular space cannot nucleate matrix assembly. Because fibronectin organises the deposition of collagens and fibrillin-1, the consequence is not the loss of one matrix component but a failure of the assembly step on which several depend. The extracellular deficit is systemic as well as local: circulating fibronectin is reduced in patient plasma.

edges.description: Mutant mesenchymal stem cells condense poorly, express fewer chondrogenic markers, and proliferate less on differentiation to chondrocytes.

edges.description: Failure of condensation and chondrogenesis at the growth plate is the cellular route from the secretion defect to the metaphyseal lesion. The intervening growth-plate steps are not directly observed in this system, which uses patient-derived cells rather than growth-plate tissue.
Disordered matrix assembly at the growth plate produces irregular metaphyseal ossification, the primary radiographic lesion.
edges.source: Deficient Extracellular Matrix Assembly in Cartilage and Bone

edges.description: Fibronectin is a systemic matrix protein, not a skeletal one, and circulating levels are reduced in patients — so extraskeletal consequences are expected in principle. GeneReviews recommends annual intraocular-pressure and blood-pressure surveillance in FN1-related disease specifically, which is a clinical recognition of that expectation. No mechanism has been worked out for either, which is why the edge carries unknown intermediates.
edges.source: Deficient Extracellular Matrix Assembly in Cartilage and Bone

edges.description: A single reported patient had generalised skeletal fragility with low-trauma bilateral femoral fractures, which the authors take as a signal that fibronectin may also maintain bone strength. This is one observation in one patient and is curated as a hypothesis, not an established feature.

edges.description: The flake-like, triangular, or curvilinear marginal ossification centres that name the disorder are the direct radiographic read-out of this node.
Disordered ossification across the growth plates reduces stature, one of the general features of the spondylometaphyseal dysplasias.
Alongside the metaphyseal lesion, ovoid vertebral bodies, developmental coxa vara, and severe scoliosis make up the secondary skeletal phenotype.
The vertebral body shape abnormality of the dysplasia.
Severe scoliosis in most individuals with FN1 variants, one of the two features separating them from classical Sutcliffe-type SMD.
Postnatal reduction of the femoral neck-shaft angle, rare within the FN1 group but pointing away from the classical entity when present.
The coxa vara and the limb malalignment together produce the waddling gait that is often the presenting sign in early childhood.
Progressive deformity restricts joint range, described as common and a major contributor to functional burden.
The vertebral dysplasia extends to the craniocervical junction, where it manifests as atlantoaxial instability requiring surgical assessment.

Odontoid anomaly has been reported once, in a girl who presented at 11.9 years with acute quadriparesis from cord compression. Vertebral change is established in this disorder and the odontoid is a vertebral ossification centre, but the report is explicit that odontoid abnormalities had not previously been described here, so a single case cannot establish the link as a regular consequence.
Generalised skeletal fragility with low-trauma bilateral femoral fractures in one reported child. Distinct from the pseudo-fractures that name the disorder.
Severe spinal osteoporosis diagnosed at 52 in a woman with a childhood SMDCF diagnosis, presenting to an adult endocrine clinic.
Limb pain persisting from childhood into the sixth decade. Whether it tracks bone strength, the metaphyseal lesion, or the deformity is not established.
Raised intraocular pressure with reported glaucoma; the trabecular meshwork is a fibronectin-rich outflow structure, which is a plausible but untested route.
Hypertension requiring management in some patients, with no established mechanism in this disorder.
The assay establishes the molecular consequence of the disease alleles directly, in both a fragment and a full-length context.
edges.limitations: A transfected recombinant system in a non-skeletal cell background. It shows that the variants block secretion, not that a secretion deficit is sufficient to produce the metaphyseal lesion in a growth plate; no skeletal cell or animal model of these alleles has been reported.

nodes.description: Irregularly shaped metaphyses carrying flake-like, triangular, or curvilinear ossification centres at their edges. The appearance simulates a healing corner fracture, which is the source of the disorder's name and of its main diagnostic hazard: a child with these radiographs has repeatedly been investigated for non-accidental injury. The changes involve the distal tibia, the ulnar aspect of the distal radius, and the proximal humerus and femur, and in at least one patient the distal femoral changes healed with skeletal maturation.

nodes.description: Mesenchymal condensation is the first committed step of skeletogenesis, and it fails in FN1-mutant cells. The proximate reason appears to be a shortfall of TGF-beta-1, which mutant cells express at significantly lower levels and which condensation requires. The finding is reversible in vitro: supplying either exogenous fibronectin or TGF-beta-1 restores condensation and promotes chondrogenesis, which makes this the first identified point of pharmacological leverage in the disorder.

nodes.description: Undegraded fibronectin-and-chaperone vesicles build up in the cytosol of patient-derived mesenchymal stem cells, a subset acquiring lysosomal markers. Cellular stress markers rise and mitochondrial structure is altered, and bulk RNA sequencing shows a transcriptomic profile specific to the patient cells. This is the second arm of the mechanism, distinct from simple extracellular deficiency: the mutant protein does harm inside the cell as well as failing to act outside it, which is the strongest argument yet that the disorder is not plain haploinsufficiency.
